extracted.intended_audience: improvisers and improv students (especially performers/students of Annoyance Theatre and those practicing Mick Napier's contrarian improv approach)
extracted.subtask_description: A training/performance rubric for improvisational actors following Mick Napier's Annoyance Theatre philosophy: contrarian, humor-first improv that prioritizes strong personal choices, using discomfort, and embracing conflict rather than following beginner 'rules'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take care of YOURSELF in the scene first
rubrics_metrics.description: The improviser's job is to take care of THEMSELVES first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A player who takes care of themselves takes care of the scene; someone obsessed with serving others becomes paralyzed. Evaluate whether your choices prioritize your own clarity, impulses, and comedic aims rather than deferring to partners. Anti-pattern: excessive people-pleasing or constantly deferring to 'make your partner look good' at the expense of boldness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make a strong initial choice without waiting for permission
rubrics_metrics.description: Make a strong choice in the first beat. ANY choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim the scene immediately rather than waiting for permission or consensus. The timing (first beat) and decisiveness of the choice matter; even a 'wrong' choice can be effective if it's strong. Scoring note: strength and immediacy are valued over cautious correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strength of choice matters more than its rightness
rubrics_metrics.description: The strength of the choice matters more than its rightness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer bold, committed choices that drive the scene forward over tentative or 'correct' ones. A strong, potentially risky choice creates clear direction and payoffs; a timid but 'accurate' choice often stalls the scene. Use commitment to amplify comedic potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use discomfort as data; do something with it
rubrics_metrics.description: If you feel uncomfortable in a scene, DO something with the discomfort, don't tamp it down.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat shared discomfort as material rather than smoothing it away. Name or act on the discomfort — doing so can reveal truth and create the funniest moments. Anti-pattern: smoothing over discomfort to maintain false safety, which often flattens comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optimize directly for funny
rubrics_metrics.description: The Annoyance is unembarrassed to optimize directly for funny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize humor as an explicit metric rather than hiding behind euphemisms like 'honesty' or 'game.' Make choices aimed at comedic payoff. Scoring note: evaluate whether actions were taken with the intent to maximize laughs, and whether that resulted in stronger scenes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow real resistance / conflict (use 'no' when appropriate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes 'no' is the strongest move; a scene where one player legitimately resists creates real conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embrace truthful resistance — conflict played truthfully is the engine of comedy. Saying 'no' can generate stakes and comedic friction; avoid obliging every offer. Anti-pattern: automatic agreement that removes tension and flattens the scene's comedic potential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be free of rules-anxiety / discard beginner scaffolding
rubrics_metrics.description: "Yes, And" is overrated. So is "Make Your Partner Look Good." Rules are scaffolding for beginners that experienced players should discard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether performers are operating out of anxiety about supposed 'improv rules' rather than making organic, bold choices. Freedom from rules-anxiety means not defaulting to textbook responses when a more interesting, rule-breaking move is available. Scoring note: look for independence from formulaic behaviors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make a strong choice in the first beat (working rubric phrasing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Did you make a strong initial choice without waiting for permission?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This restates the initiation expectation as an evaluative question: check for decisiveness, immediate scene claim, and avoidance of permission-seeking. Use this as a quick observable metric when rating openings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use discomfort (working rubric phrasing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Did you USE discomfort rather than smoothing it?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this item as a concrete evaluative prompt: when discomfort appears, did the player act on it (naming it, escalating it, mining it) instead of neutralizing it?

rubrics_metrics.name: Optimize for funny (working rubric phrasing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Are you optimizing directly for funny?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether choices were intentionally aimed at comedic effect. This prompt helps keep 'funny' as the explicit success metric rather than a euphemistic proxy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow resistance/conflict (working rubric phrasing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Did you allow real resistance / conflict?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this checklist item to verify presence and truthfulness of opposition or pushback in the scene; note whether resistance generated stakes and comedic interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom from rules-anxiety (working rubric phrasing)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for signs of anxiety-driven, rule-following behavior (over-reliance on 'yes, and', forced support moves). Reward players who act beyond prescriptive rules in service of clearer, funnier scenes.
